body:
After further investigation, here's the results on this issue (at least, AFAIK). > **TL;DR**: after calling `ObjectDB::unregister_core_types()`, `object_slots` in `object.cpp` became a dangling pointer, which caused Godot to crash when accessing it. This happens when we create ANYTHING that inherits from `Object` Class, one of which is `RefCounted`, which we use when writing to `benchmark_results.txt` file through `FileAccess::open` with Write permissions. > A possible solution is to re-order the execution, so we write to our file **_then_** we free (unregister) the core types, but in this solution, we won't be able to write results of benchmark of unregistration, which isn't ideal tbh.
Details of How this happened

we call `benchmark_dump` on line `5275` (on commit https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/c12e51972a41665743be79c7d3e3fd5c871d97f3), with benchmark_file being set (we want to write the results to a file, not to stdout). We try creating a new Refcounted object with `FileAccess::open`, returning type is `Ref`, inside `benchmark_dump` function, as `Refcounted` inherits `Object` we'll try to call `add_instance` inside `core/object/object.cpp` file upon construction, `object.cpp` utilizes `object_slots`, a Vector-like dynamic array (realloc when size == max_size, with the new size equal to max_size * 2). If, by any chance, object_slots is a dangling pointer, or equal to nullptr, it'll crash Godot as we're doing undefined behaviour in line `2462` of `object.cpp` file, this line tries to access memory that isn't ours, which's forbidden and will punish you with a very harsh, and unforgiven segfault, or in c++ case, a thrown exception. Now why would `object_slots` be an invalid pointer? it's because we freed it with `memfree(object_slots)` in `ObjectDB::cleanup()` function, this function is called in `ObjectDB::unregister_core_types()`, which's called in `Main::cleanup()`, note that `Main::cleanup()` is only called when you try exiting Godot. If we look at the `Main::cleanup()` code, we'll see that we call unregister_core_types function FIRST, then we call the benchmarks_dump function afterward, which if we recall, calling unregister_core_types would make any attempt at creating new Objects pretty much impossible, due to the reasons explained above. https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/c12e51972a41665743be79c7d3e3fd5c871d97f3/main/main.cpp#L5272-L5275 a quick solution is to reorder some operations so that `benchmarks_dump` function First, then we call unregister_core_types to give back memory to the OS. Now.. it would be an easy fix, if we didn't encounter a cyclic relation problem, as we're benchmarking unregister_core_types function.. but we never write the results to our benchmark_file. sadly, from what I can tell, it would require too much effort to make it work (i.e. making what gets printed to stdout == whats inside benchmark_file), and I doubt it would be needed, as this bug went (seemingly) unnoticed since 831b4a5366caf8a0202b2ac2fad641505282915c was merged (which added/improved this system as we know it). a quick workaround is to check if ObjectDB's object_slots is valid or not (object_slots is null or not) and printing the results to stdout if it's invalid, with a note saying "we couldn't write the results to benchmark_file due to XYZ".
